What does Manton say is required for a person to attain true blessedness?

Manton teaches that true blessedness is attained only when the teaching of God prevails upon the heart and completely fills it, and that seeking blessedness in temporal things is a serious error. He warns that "It is not only an affront put upon God, but also a great wrong, to neglect the word of God, and the way he prescribes, and to seek blessedness in temporal things." Moreover, he explains that "That which fills must be greater than the thing filled," indicating that only the infinite fullness of God can satisfy the chaotic desires of the human heart.

What does Sibbes say about the role of constant, strong, and growing desires in confirming a sanctified soul?

Sibbes teaches that when a person’s desires are constant and ever‑increasing, they serve as evidence of a sanctified frame of soul and a new creature. He explains that such desires are not fleeting like a torrent but are perpetual, and they " Strong and growing desires argue the truth of desires ; as indeed a child of God hath never grace enough, never i^ith enough, never love enough, or comfort enough, till he come to heaven, ihey are growing desires more and more." In this view, holy desires spring from a holy soul and point toward the ultimate fulfillment of all promises in heaven.

What does Richard Mather say true joining to the church involves, as opposed to merely hearing the Word or having affection for the congregation?

Richard Mather teaches that true joining to the church is not simply dwelling in the town, hearing the Word, or expressing affection, but requires a voluntary covenantal fellowship. He explains that “it must be meant of joyning in that neere relation of Church-fellowship amongst them, so as to be engaged by volun tary consent and agreement to be members of their Church.” Thus, genuine membership is grounded in a conscious, covenantal agreement rather than mere attendance or emotional approval.

How does Watson contrast Christ's opening of the Sermon on the Mount with the giving of the Law on Sinai?

Watson teaches that Christ begins the Sermon on the Mount with promises and blessings rather than with commands and threatenings. Where the Law on the mount came with trumpet, flame, quaking earth, and fear, the Saviour whose lips dropped as the honeycomb opens with sweet, ravishing doctrine that draws even hard hearts.

Why does Manton say Christians should highly esteem the Lord's Prayer, and are they absolutely tied to its exact form?

Manton teaches that the Lord's Prayer was formed and indited by Christ, who as the wisdom of God knew both our necessities and the Father's good-will, and so gave a perfect form and directory. He adds that believers are not absolutely tied to that form; the apostles' recorded prayers do not show them using it as a fixed liturgy.

What metaphor does Flavel recommend for describing the church’s deliverance, and how does he illustrate it with natural imagery?

Flavel teaches that believers should favor metaphors that the Spirit has authorized in Scripture, using the image of spring to portray the church’s deliverance. He writes, "In the spring, the earth, Hke a most bountiful parent, opens her bosom, produces variety of herbs, adorns the meadows with abundance of flowers ;" to show how nature’s renewal reflects the joy and freedom God brings to His people.

What reason does Thomas Gouge give for believers to give alms of their possessions?

Thomas Gouge teaches that believers should give alms because doing so makes all things clean and sanctified for them. He writes, "Give alms of such things as you have, and behold all things are clean unto you:" and argues that this act aligns with the apostolic inference that charitable giving secures and sanctifies the rest of one's goods. Moreover, Gouge stresses that people are "Stewards, than Lords and Owners of this worlds goods; all is the Lords," so giving alms reflects proper stewardship and brings God's blessing.

According to Sibbes in Works Vol04, how should a person's particular calling relate to their love for God?

Sibbes teaches that love of God must be expressed through the specific duties and offices each person holds, not as an abstract feeling. He writes that the command to love God "must love God ' with all our mind^ with all our heart, with all our power and strength,' Deut. vi. 5 ; that is, in our particular places" applies to each individual’s role, whether magistrate, minister, or statesman, so that love is demonstrated in the performance of those responsibilities. Sibbes further asks, "How far doth thy activity, thy power, thy sphere, that thou canst do anj'thing, stretch ? So far must thy love ; and thou must shew thy love in all the powers and abilities that God hath fur'- nished thee with," emphasizing that love to God is discovered in action within one's calling.

In Herbert's Affliction poem, what does the speaker try to offer to warm God's love, and what happens to that offering?

Herbert's speaker goes to fetch a sacrifice from his fold, thinking that presenting it would warm love he feared had grown cold. As he tenders his heart, the man who should receive it slips his hand and throws the heart into the scalding pan—so the intended offering becomes the speaker's own suffering.

What does Guthrie say the new principle of life requires regarding sin and obedience to God’s commands?

Guthrie teaches that the new principle of life, by the good hand of God, makes a person set himself against every known sin, refusing to allow any darkness a peaceful abode, and to "respect all God's known commands;" to "live godly, righteously, and soberly" while pressing forward toward the mark for the prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus. He illustrates this radical rejection of sin with the biblical admonition "If thy right eye offend thee, pluck it out, and cast it from thee," and reminds believers that "What fellowship hath righteousness with unrighteousness? and what communion hath light with darkness?"

According to Watson, what is God's response to a good intention compared to an intentional wicked act?

Watson teaches that God is attentive to the motives behind human actions, rewarding sincere good intentions while punishing deliberate wickedness. He writes, "If there be but a good intention, God takes notice," and contrasts this with the statement that "God punifheth in‑tentional wicked nefs, and crowns intentional goodnefs." Thus, the divine observation is not merely of outward deeds but of the heart’s purpose, granting favor to those whose inner desire aligns with righteousness and condemning those who willfully choose evil.

What does Greenham say is the primary desire of a true servant of God, and how should that desire shape his prayer?

Greenham teaches that the true servant’s primary desire is the statutes of God, not worldly riches or kingdoms. He writes, "though the whole earth be full of mercie, yet he desireth onely the statutes of God," and stresses that "He prayeth chiefly for the teaching of the Spirit, without which hee should erre." Thus, a believer should remember God’s goodness, seek the teaching of the Spirit in accordance with the Word, and pray for that divine instruction above all other requests.

According to Boston’s Fourfold State, why does the natural man fail to obey the holy law even when he seems to love it?

Boston explains that the natural man may claim a kind of love for the law, but he "looks on the holy law in -a carnal dress" and therefore does not perceive its true spirituality. Because he sees the law only in a fleshly form, he "thinks he has the law, but in very deed he is without the law," and his unrenewed will is averse to good, with "Sin is the natural man's element" that he is loath to part with. Consequently, without the power of grace to change his will, he cannot comply with the law.

How does Goodwin in Works Vol02 describe the status of Christians who live in the same lusts as the Gentiles?

Goodwin teaches that Christians who live in the same lusts as the Gentiles are considered no different from the Gentiles before God, stating that "they shall all be reckoned as Gentiles before God." This classification is based on their continued indulgence in fleshly desires, which he equates with the Gentile way of life.

He writes, "So sweet are these comforts of the Spirit that they do much abate and moderate our joy in worldly things," indicating that once a Christian has tasted the sweetness of the Lord, the desire for earthly delights wanes.

What definition does Goodwin give for the glory of heaven and which creature does he cite as the only truly glorious one?

Goodwin teaches that glory is essentially "first aU excellences whatsoever ; and all excellences in the height, and such a weight as they do oppress, that the ordinary understanding of man cannot bear." He explains that this super‑excellence applies to beauty, strength, joy, and holiness, surpassing any human imagination. To illustrate a concrete example, Goodwin notes that "the world hath but one thing, that is a creature, that truly deserveth the name of being glorious, and that is the sun."

What does Durham describe as the nature of the union between Christ and believers?

Durham teaches that the union between Christ the Bridegroom and believers the Bride is a mutual giving in which neither party retains independent power. He explains that the Bridegroom has no power over himself when he is married to the Bride, and likewise the Bride has no power over herself apart from the Bridegroom. This creates a in which both are bound to each other. The consent that makes the union effective comes through faith in Christ’s word, illustrated by the invitation, "Behold I stand at the door and knock, if any man will hear my voice and open the door, I will come in to him, and will sup with him, and he with me". Thus believers are called to relinquish self‑mastery and be wholly at Christ’s disposal.

What does Sibbes say about God's attitude toward sin before it is committed?

Sibbes explains that before the commission of sin, God does not command it nor infuse it, but rather "disallow and forbid it." He emphasizes that God is not the author of evil, yet He orders and directs it, distinguishing three stages of sin: before the commission, in the act, and upon its performance.

How does the sermon advise Christians to exercise their voting rights in civil elections?

The sermon teaches that believers should not abandon their citizenship but should vote responsibly, seeking God’s guidance and acknowledging accountability. It urges that they use the right of voting "in the sight of Almighty God," recognizing that they will be brought into account for their choices. Moreover, it reminds them that "we are our own governors, to a great degree," and therefore must exercise prudence and prayer to make a right choice.

According to the sermon, where was Moses when he prayed the words “Lord, thou hast been our dwelling‑place in all generations”?

Spurgeon observes that Moses was "in the wilderness; not in some of the halls of Pharaoh, nor yet in a habitation in the land of Goshen; but in a wilderness." He explains that from that remote setting Moses looked upon the traveling Israelites and lifted his eyes to declare that God had been their dwelling‑place through every generation.

What does Spurgeon teach about the relationship between the church's binding and loosing actions on earth and in heaven?

Spurgeon teaches that the authority exercised by the church in binding and loosing is effective both on earth and in heaven, for he writes, "What they have bound on earth is bound in Heaven. What they have loosed on earth is also loosed in Heaven." This shows that the decisions of godly assemblies carry heavenly weight, and that when genuine repentance is expressed the bond is loosed on earth and also in Heaven. He also highlights the power of a prayer meeting of two believers, citing Jesus' promise, "Again I say unto you, that if two of you," which demonstrates that even a very small gathering can invoke divine response.

How does Sermon 116 describe the relationship between sins we notice and the secret sins we are unaware of?

Spurgeon teaches that the sins we notice are only a small portion of our total unholiness, comparing them to “the farmer's small samples which he brings to market, when he has left his granary full at home.” He asserts that “sin is sin, whether we see it or not,” so secret sins are just as real, though they lack the aggravation of willfulness.

What reason does Spurgeon give in Sermon 1291 for why bearing the yoke in youth is advantageous?

Spurgeon teaches that submitting to God's yoke while still young prepares a person for a life of useful service, just as a young animal must be broken early to become a reliable worker. He explains that the burden may be uncomfortable, but it is profitable, and illustrates the point by noting that "If the bullock is not broken when it is young, it will never make a good plowing ox." By being “broken” in youth, believers develop the strength and obedience needed for later ministry.

Why does Gill say that the knowledge of God is incommunicable to creatures?

Gill teaches that the knowledge of God is incommunicable because it is inseparable from God’s own nature: “it is his nature and essence, and therefore is incommunicable to a creature.” Since this knowledge is essential to the divine essence, no created being, even the human nature of Christ, can partake of it, and therefore it remains beyond the grasp of any creature.

How does Shedd argue that our moral feelings point to divine attributes in Dogmatic Theology Volume 3?

Shedd teaches that the awareness of our own moral feelings moves the mind toward the conception of divine attributes, noting that we are led “to the conception of the existence of attributes the same in kind, however exalted in degree, in the Divine Being.” In other words, the moral sense within humanity reflects a likeness to the moral qualities of God, though God's attributes are infinitely higher. This reasoning supports the broader claim that the order and constancy observed in nature reveal a unified, intelligent will governing the universe.

Why does Gill begin his Body of Doctrinal Divinity with the Being of God and the proof of it?

Gill teaches that theology is a discoursing concerning God—his nature, names, perfections, persons, purposes, providences, ways, works, and word—so he begins with God's being and its evidence as the foundation of all religion. If there were no God, religion would be vain, and neither belief nor practice would matter, for there would be no superior Being to whom we are accountable.

What reason does Dabney give for rejecting utility as the sole basis of moral obligation?

Dabney argues that moral obligation cannot rest on utility because conscience condemns secret sins that produce no outward loss, and he emphasizes that “the morality of the act is not in its utility, but in its rational motive.” He therefore concludes that virtue must be grounded in rational motives rather than merely in the usefulness of an action.

How does Gill describe the difference between God's truth and human truth?

Gill teaches that God's truth is unchanging and eternal, contrasting it with the mutable nature of human understanding. He states that “It is immutable and invariable, as he himself, as his nature is; truth does not always appear in the same light to men; at first more obscurely, then more clearly; it has its gradations and increase; but in God is always the same.” Thus, while human truth can appear in varying degrees of clarity, God’s truth remains constant, faithful, and true “yesterday, today, and for ever.”

What arguments does the author give for interpreting the antichrist in the passage as an ecclesiastical power rather than a civil one?

The author argues that several considerations point to an ecclesiastical interpretation. First, the designations "man of sin" and "son of perdition" are described as having a religious import, which makes them more appropriate to an ecclesiastical than a worldly power. These reasons together support the view that the antichrist is an ecclesiastical power.
